subject: devops
question: Which command downloads an image from a registry without starting a container?
explanation: docker pull downloads an image from a registry; docker run would pull it implicitly and also start a container.

subject: devops
question: Which Dockerfile instruction sets the default command that runs when a container starts, unless arguments override it?
explanation: CMD provides the default command; RUN executes at build time, not when the container starts.

subject: devops
question: Which command uploads a tagged local image to a registry?
explanation: docker push sends the image's layers to the registry named in its tag.

subject: devops
question: Which Dockerfile instruction sets the base image for a build?
explanation: FROM must be the first instruction (aside from ARG) and names the image the build starts from.

subject: devops
question: Which command lists the images stored locally on your machine?
explanation: docker images lists local images with repository, tag, ID, and size.

subject: devops
question: What is the purpose of a .dockerignore file?
options: It sets environment variables for containers
It excludes matching files from the build context sent to the daemon
It defines the container's startup command
explanation: Files matched by .dockerignore are not sent with the build context, which keeps builds faster and images cleaner.

subject: devops
question: Which Dockerfile instruction sets the directory that later RUN, CMD, COPY, and similar instructions use as their working directory?
explanation: WORKDIR sets, and creates if needed, the working directory for subsequent instructions and the container.

subject: devops
question: When a Dockerfile defines both ENTRYPOINT and CMD in exec form, how are they combined?
options: ENTRYPOINT sets the executable, and CMD supplies default arguments that docker run arguments can replace
Only the instruction written last takes effect
ENTRYPOINT runs at build time and CMD runs at start time
explanation: Arguments passed to docker run replace CMD and are appended to the ENTRYPOINT.

subject: devops
question: Which command shows the layers that make up an image, along with their sizes and the commands that created them?
explanation: docker history lists each layer of an image with the instruction that produced it and its size.

subject: devops
question: Why is the exec form CMD ["node", "server.js"] usually preferred over the shell form CMD node server.js?
options: The process runs directly as PID 1 and receives signals such as SIGTERM, instead of being wrapped in /bin/sh -c
Shell form cannot read environment variables
Exec form makes the build cache more effective
explanation: With shell form, the shell becomes PID 1 and may not forward stop signals to the app.

subject: devops
question: Which practice keeps apt package lists out of a Debian-based image?
options: Install packages in one RUN and delete apt lists in a later RUN
Use COPY instead of RUN to install packages
Install and remove apt lists within the same RUN instruction
Set ENV APT_CACHE=0 at the top of the file
explanation: Files deleted in a later layer still exist in the earlier layer, so cleanup must happen in the same RUN that created them.

subject: devops
question: Why copy package.json and run npm install before copying the rest of the application source in a Node Dockerfile?
options: Dependencies are reinstalled on every source change
The dependency layer can be cached until package.json changes
Source files are excluded from the image
It makes the final image smaller
explanation: Source edits invalidate only the layers after the COPY of the source, so the slow npm install layer stays cached.

subject: devops
question: Why does Docker reuse cached layers during a build?
options: Layers are compressed into a single file on every build
Docker caches all layers globally across machines by default
Each instruction that is unchanged, along with its inputs, produces the same layer, so it is reused
The cache is used only for the base image
explanation: If an instruction and its inputs have not changed, Docker reuses the layer it produced last time; a change invalidates that layer and every layer after it.
